title: Fossils
seo_title: Year 6 Science: Fossils Worksheets (How Fossils Form, Rock Layers, Mary Anning)
standard_text: Recognise that living things have changed over time and that fossils provide information about living things that inhabited the Earth millions of years ago.
meta_desc: Free Year 6 science worksheets on fossils: how fossils form, body and trace fossils, rock layers, what fossils tell us, timelines and Mary Anning. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Fossils are clues from millions of years ago.
key_sub: Deeper rock layers are older; fossils show how life has changed.
body_html:
How to think about it

Fossils are the remains or traces of living things preserved in rock.

  • A body is buried quickly in mud or sand; soft parts rot; layers press into rock; minerals replace the bones over millions of years.
  • Body fossils are bones, shells and teeth; trace fossils are footprints, burrows and dung.
  • In undisturbed layers, deeper rock is older. Fossils show that living things and places have changed over time.
Example

Fossil A is in the top layer, fossil B at the bottom. Older?

New layers form on top

Answer: fossil B

Example

230 and 66 million years ago. Difference?

230 − 66

Answer: 164 million years

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the top layer is the oldest.
  • Thinking a footprint cannot be a fossil.
  • Thinking people and dinosaurs lived at the same time.

faq.a: A living thing is buried quickly in mud or sand. Its soft parts rot, the sediment hardens into rock, and over millions of years minerals replace the hard parts.

faq.q: How do we know which fossils are older?
faq.a: In undisturbed rock, layers build up on top of each other, so fossils in deeper layers are older than those above.
A fossil hunter from Lyme Regis in Dorset who, in the early 1800s, found ichthyosaur and plesiosaur skeletons that changed how scientists thought about the past.

The soft parts rot away, leaving bones or shell.
items.e: Order: dies → covered → soft parts rot → layers press → minerals replace → found.
